source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2
notes_on_source: Verses 48 and 51 are missing from the source.

verses.translation: And Yeshua traveled{H5265} from there and came{H935} to the land{H776} of Yehudah{H3063}, beyond the river{H5104} Yarden{H3383}; and a great{H7227} people{H5971} gathered{H622} there, and he taught{H1875} them as his custom{H4941}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דורש (doresh — 'expounds/interprets', from דרש H1875 — 'to seek/inquire/expound'). This is the specific rabbinic term for Torah exposition — the same root as מדרש (midrash). Greek has ἐδίδασκεν ('he taught'). A back-translator from 'taught' would use לימד (limed), not the midrashic exposition verb.

verses.translation: And the Separatists{H6504} asked{H7592} him, testing{H5254} him: Can a man{H376} leave{H5800} his wife{H802}?
And Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559} to them: What did Moshe{H4872} command{H6680} you?
And they said{H559}: Moshe{H4872} permitted{H5414} that a man{H120} write{H3789} her a letter{H5612} of divorce{H3748} and send her away{H5117}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ספר כריתות (sefer keritut — 'letter of cutting-off/divorce', H5612 + H3748). The root כרת (karat — 'to cut') gives divorce its Hebrew meaning: a CUTTING of the covenant bond. Greek has βιβλίον ἀποστασίου ('certificate of standing-apart/abandonment'). The Hebrew frames divorce as cutting a covenant (like כרת ברית — 'cutting a covenant'); the Greek frames it as departure/standing apart. These are different conceptual metaphors that would not cross in translation.
This is a direct reference to Deuteronomy 24:1: 'he shall write her a letter of divorce (ספר כריתת).' The Hebrew preserves the Deuteronomic legal terminology verbatim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'letter of cutting-off' (כריתות — covenant-cutting). Greek: 'certificate of standing-apart' (ἀποστάσιον — departure/divorce). Different metaphors for the same legal act.
translation_notes: 'Letter of divorce' for sefer keritut — literally 'scroll of cutting.' The divorce document cuts the marriage covenant.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 24:1: 'When a man takes a wife and marries her, if she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found some indecency in her, he shall write her a letter of divorce (ספר כריתת) and put it in her hand and send her out of his house.'

verses.translation: And to them Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559}: He permitted it to you because of the wickedness{H7455} of your hearts{H3824}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רוע לבבכם (ro'a levavkhem — 'the wickedness of your hearts'). Greek has πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν ('for your hardness of heart'). Hebrew: the heart is WICKED (רע — evil/bad). Greek: the heart is HARD (σκληρός). Different moral diagnoses: moral corruption vs. emotional stubbornness.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'wickedness of your hearts' (רוע — moral evil). Greek: 'hardness of your hearts' (σκληροκαρδία — stubbornness). Different heart conditions.

verses.translation: But HaShem{H8034} formed{H3335} in the beginning{H7225} of the world{H8398}, male{H2145} and female{H5347}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יצר (yatzar — 'formed/fashioned', H3335) — the specific creation verb from Genesis 2:7 (ויצר יהוה אלהים את האדם — 'and YHWH God formed the man'). Greek has ἐποίησεν ('made'). A back-translator from 'made' would use עשה (asah — 'made'), not the potter-verb יצר. The Hebrew author reaches for the Genesis 2 formation vocabulary — God as the potter fashioning humanity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'formed' (יצר — potter's craft, Gen 2:7). Greek: 'made' (ἐποίησεν — general creation). Different creation vocabulary.
textual_notes: Genesis 1:27: 'male and female he created them.' Genesis 2:7: 'YHWH God formed (ויצר) man from the dust of the ground.' The Hebrew combines both Genesis accounts.

verses.translation: And a man{H120} shall leave{H5800} his father{H1} and his mother{H517} and take{H3947} a wife{H802}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ויקח אשה (ve-yiqach ishah — 'and take a wife'). The OT Genesis 2:24 and the Greek both say 'and shall cleave to his wife' (ודבק באשתו / κολληθήσεται πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ). The Hebrew Gospel substitutes 'take' (לקח) for 'cleave' (דבק). A back-translator from Greek would preserve 'cleave.' The Hebrew uses the common OT idiom for marriage: לקח אשה ('to take a wife' — Gen 4:19, 6:2, 11:29, 12:19).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'and take a wife' (לקח — marriage idiom). Greek: 'and shall cleave to his wife' (κολλάω — adhesion). Different verbs, both expressing marriage but from different perspectives.

verses.translation: And the two{H8147} of them shall become one{H259} flesh{H1320}.

textual_notes: Genesis 2:24 verbatim: 'and they shall become one flesh' (והיו לבשר אחד).

verses.translation: And what God{H410} joins{H2266}, no man{H120} shall separate{H6504}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יפריד (yafrid — 'shall separate', from פרד H6504 — the root of 'Pharisee' פרושים). Yeshua uses the Pharisee-root verb: 'No man shall pharisee-ize/separate what God has joined.' The irony: the Separatists ask about divorce (separation), and Yeshua says separation is forbidden — using their own root word against them.

verses.translation: And again they asked{H7592} him in the house{H1004}.
And he said{H559} to them: Whoever leaves{H5117} his wife{H802} and takes{H3947} another{H312} commits adultery{H5003}.
And if the wife{H802} leaves{H5800} her husband{H1167}, she commits adultery{H5003}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בעלה (ba'alah — 'her lord/husband', H1167). בעל (ba'al) means 'lord/master/owner' and is the standard Hebrew word for husband emphasizing authority. Greek has τὸν ἄνδρα αὐτῆς ('her man/husband'). The Hebrew preserves the patriarchal marriage structure embedded in the language.

verses.translation: And the peoples{H5971} sent{H7971} him a gift{H1890} of youths{H5288}, that he might touch{H5060} them; and the disciples were preventing{H4513} those who sent{H7971} them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דורון (doron — 'gift/present', H1890). Greek has προσέφερον αὐτῷ παιδία ('they brought children to him'). The Hebrew frames the children as a GIFT presented to the teacher — an offering of young souls. A back-translator from 'brought' would use הביאו (hevi'u — 'they brought'), not the gift-giving word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sent him a gift of youths' (דורון — gift/offering). Greek: 'they brought children to him' (προσφέρω — present/bring). Different framing: gift vs. presentation.

verses.translation: And when Yeshua saw{H7200} it, he was full{H4392} of wrath{H2534} and said{H559} to them: Let{H5117} the youths{H5288} come{H935} to me and do not prevent{H4513} them, for of such is the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חימה (chemah — 'wrath/fury', H2534) — the OT word for divine fury (Deut 29:27, 2 Kings 22:13, Isa 51:17, Jer 25:15). Greek has ἠγανάκτησεν ('was indignant/annoyed'). Hebrew: full of WRATH. Greek: indignant. The Hebrew emotion is far stronger — this is the anger of God, not mere annoyance. A back-translator from 'indignant' would use כעס (ka'as — 'vexed'), not the divine-fury word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'full of wrath' (חימה — divine fury). Greek: 'was indignant' (ἀγανακτέω — annoyed). Much stronger emotion in Hebrew.

verses.translation: Truly{H571} I say{H559} to you: No man{H120} shall enter{H935} the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064} unless he is humble{H8217} and blameless{H8549} and becomes like a youth{H5288}.

one_way_hebrew: Adds שפל ותמים (shafal ve-tamim — 'humble and blameless') — two qualities absent from Greek. Greek simply says 'whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a child' (ὡς παιδίον). The Hebrew adds TWO specific moral qualities: שפל (shafal, H8217 — 'lowly/humble', the opposite of proud) and תמים (tamim, H8549 — 'blameless/whole/perfect' — the word used for Noah in Gen 6:9 and for sacrificial animals without blemish). A back-translator from Greek would not add these OT-loaded qualities.

תמים (tamim — 'blameless/complete', H8549) is the word YHWH uses for Abraham: 'Walk before me and be tamim' (Gen 17:1). Also the requirement for Passover lambs (Ex 12:5) and all sacrifices (Lev 1:3, 3:1). The kingdom requires the wholeness of a sacrificial lamb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'humble and blameless' (שפל ותמים) — absent from Greek, which only has the child comparison.

verses.translation: And Yeshua embraced{H2263} them and laid{H5117} his hands{H3027} upon them and blessed{H1288} them.

And as he was going out{H3318} on the way{H1870}, a certain man{H120} came{H935} and knelt{H3766} before him, asking{H1245} and saying{H559}: Good{H2896} teacher{H3925}, what shall we do{H6213} that we may obtain{H5381} the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses נעשה (na'aseh — 'shall WE do', first person plural). Greek has τί ποιήσω ('what shall I do', first person singular). The Hebrew man speaks inclusively — 'what shall WE do?' — whereas the Greek is individual. The Hebrew framing is communal.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'what shall we do to obtain the kingdom of heaven?' (communal, with 'kingdom of heaven'). Greek: 'what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' (individual, with 'eternal life'). Different goals and different scope.

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to him: Why do you call{H559} me good{H2896}? No man{H120} is good{H2896} except{H905} God{H410} alone.

You know{H3045} the commandments{H4687} of HaShem{H8034}: You shall not commit adultery{H5003}, you shall not murder{H7523}, you shall not steal{H1589}, you shall not give false{H8267} testimony{H5707}, you shall not oppress{H3238} any man{H120}, honor{H3513} your father{H1} and your mother{H517}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לא תונה שום אדם (lo toneh shum adam — 'you shall not oppress any man', from ינה/הונה H3238 — 'to oppress/wrong/defraud'). This is the specific Torah verb for oppressing the stranger and the vulnerable (Ex 22:20 'You shall not oppress (לא תונה) a stranger'; Lev 19:33, 25:14,17; Deut 23:17). Greek has μὴ ἀποστερήσῃς ('do not defraud'). The Hebrew verb carries the full weight of Torah's protection of the weak; the Greek is narrower (financial fraud).

verses.translation: And he answered{H6030} and said{H559} to him: Rabbi, all{H3605} this I have kept{H6965} from my youth{H5271} until now.

And Yeshua looked at{H5027} him and it pleased{H3190} him, and he said{H559} to him: One{H259} thing{H1697} you lack{H2637} — sell{H4376} what you have and give{H5414} it to the poor{H6041}, and you shall have a great{H1419} treasure{H214} in the heavens{H8064}. And come{H935} after me.
And when he heard{H8085} this, he was saddened{H6087} and went away{H1980}; for he was a man{H376} who had many{H7227} estates{H5159}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נחלות (nachalot — 'estates/inheritances', H5159). This is the OT word for tribal land-inheritance — the allotted portions of the Promised Land (Josh 13-19, Num 26:53, 34:2, Deut 4:38). Greek has κτήματα πολλά ('many possessions'). A back-translator from 'possessions' would use קניינים or רכוש, not the land-inheritance word. The Hebrew implies the man's wealth is in ancestral land — the nachalah that belongs to the tribe.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'many estates/inheritances' (נחלות — tribal land). Greek: 'many possessions' (κτήματα — property). Different type of wealth.

verses.translation: And Yeshua turned{H2015} to his disciples and said{H559}: How impossible{H4513} a thing it is that a man{H376} who has much{H7227} money{H3701} should enter{H935} the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064}!

And the disciples were alarmed{H926} at his words{H1697}. And Yeshua a second time{H6471} immediately said{H559} to them: Children{H1121}, how very{H3966} heavy{H3515} it is that a man{H376} who trusts{H982} greatly in his riches{H6239} should be able{H3201} to enter{H935} the kingdom{H4438} of God{H410}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יבטח בעושרו (yivtach be-oshro — 'trusts in his riches', from בטח H982 — 'to trust/rely upon'). This is the OT language: Psalm 52:9 'the man who did not make God his refuge, but trusted (בטח) in the abundance of his riches'; Proverbs 11:28 'Whoever trusts (בוטח) in his riches shall fall.' Greek adds this in some manuscripts but the Hebrew's phrasing directly quotes the Psalms/Proverbs vocabulary.
textual_notes: Psalm 52:9: 'See the man who would not make God his stronghold, but trusted in the abundance of his riches.' Yeshua echoes this psalm precisely.

verses.translation: It is easier{H7043} for a camel{H1581} to pass through{H5674} the eye{H5869} of the needle{H4545} than a rich{H6223} man{H376} into the kingdom{H4438} of heaven{H8064}.
And they were astonished{H8539}, saying{H559} among themselves: If so, who{H4310} can be saved{H3467}?
And Yeshua warned{H2094}, saying{H559} to them: For you it is an impossible{H4513} thing, but not for HaShem{H8034}, for to God{H410} all{H3605} things are possible.

textual_notes: Genesis 18:14: 'Is anything too wonderful (הֲיִפָּלֵא) for YHWH?' The same theological principle.

verses.translation: And Keyfa began to say{H559} to him: Behold{H2009}, we have left{H5800} all{H3605} things and follow{H1980} after you.

And Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559}: Truly{H571} I say{H559} to you that a man{H376} who leaves{H5800} his house{H1004} and his brothers{H251} and his sisters{H269}, or father{H1} and mother{H517}, or children{H1121}, or estates{H5159}, for the sake of my love{H160} or for the sake of the good-news{H1319} —

one_way_hebrew: Uses אהבתי (ahavati — 'my love', H160). Greek has ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ ('for my sake'). The Hebrew says 'for the sake of my LOVE' — a more intimate and relational phrasing. A back-translator from 'for my sake' would write בעדי or למעני, not the love-language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'for the sake of my love' (אהבתי — personal love). Greek: 'for my sake' (ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ — on my account). More intimate in Hebrew.

verses.translation: He shall receive{H6901} a reward{H1576} a hundred{H3967} times{H6471} over, and still{H5750} in this time{H6256}: houses{H1004} and brothers{H251}, or sisters{H269}, or children{H1121} — with troubles{H6869} — and in the world{H5769} to come{H935}, eternal{H5331} life{H2416}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses העולם הבא (ha-olam ha-ba — 'the world to come'). This is the standard rabbinic eschatological term for the age of resurrection and eternal life. Greek has ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τῷ ἐρχομένῳ ('in the coming age'). While similar, the Hebrew is the native rabbinic concept from which the Greek is derived.

verses.translation: And many{H7227} first{H7223} shall be last{H314}, and the last{H314} shall be first{H7223}.

And they were then on the way{H1870}, going up{H5927} to Yerushalayim{H3389}, and Yeshua went{H1980} first{H7223}; and they were drawn{H4900} after him, astonished{H8539} and afraid{H3372}. And then once more{H6471} he said{H559} to them and began to tell{H559} all{H3605} that would happen to him.

Saying{H559}: Behold{H2009}, we go up{H5927} to Yerushalayim{H3389}, and the Son{H1121} of God{H410} shall be delivered{H4560} into the hand{H3027} of the chief{H1419} priests{H3548} and the scribes{H5608} and the elders{H2205}; and they shall sentence{H7081} him to death{H4194} and deliver{H4560} him to the Nephilim{H5303}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נפילים (Nephilim, H5303) where Greek has τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ('the gentiles/nations'). The Nephilim are the fallen ones/giants of Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33 — the violent offspring of fallen beings who filled the earth with violence. A back-translator from Greek 'gentiles' would use גוים (goyim — 'nations'), NEVER Nephilim. The Hebrew author views the Romans through the lens of the biblical Nephilim — monstrous offspring of fallen powers who rule by brute force. This is one of the most striking one-way markers in the entire Gospel.
Again uses בן האל (ben ha-El — 'Son of God') where Greek has υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man').
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Nephilim' (נפילים — fallen giants of Gen 6:4). Greek: 'gentiles' (ἔθνεσιν — nations). Completely different characterization of the Romans.
Hebrew: 'Son of God.' Greek: 'Son of Man.' Consistent pattern.
translation_notes: 'Nephilim' — the fallen ones of Genesis 6:4. The Hebrew characterizes the Roman occupiers as the biblical Nephilim: violent, powerful, and the product of spiritual corruption.
textual_notes: Genesis 6:4: 'The Nephilim were on the earth in those days... they were the mighty men of old, men of renown.' Numbers 13:33: 'We saw the Nephilim... and we were like grasshoppers in our own sight.' The Hebrew author sees Rome as the Nephilim — the giants who make Israel feel like grasshoppers.

verses.translation: And they shall mock{H3932} him and spit{H7556} upon him and strike{H5221} him and kill{H4191} him, and he shall rise{H6965} alive{H2416} on the third{H7992} day{H3117}.
And Ya'aqov{H3290} and Yochanan{H3110}, sons{H1121} of Zavdai, drew near{H7126} to him, saying{H559}: Rabbi, we want{H7521} that whatever{H3605} thing we ask{H7592}, you will do{H6213} for us.
And Yeshua said{H559} to them: What do you want{H7521} that I should do{H6213} for you?
And they said{H559}: Grant{H5414} us that one{H259} of us sit{H3427} at your right{H3225} side and the other at your left{H8040}, in your light{H216}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses באורך (be-orekha — 'in your light', from אור H216 — 'light'). Greek has ἐν τῇ δόξῃ σου ('in your glory'). Same pattern as Mark 8:38 — 'light' where Greek has 'glory.' The Hebrew associates the kingdom with divine light (Gen 1:3, Ps 104:2 'wrapped in light as a garment'); the Greek associates it with glory/honor. A back-translator from 'glory' would use בכבודך.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in your light' (אור). Greek: 'in your glory' (δόξα). Consistent pattern.

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to them: You do not know{H3045} what you are asking{H7592}. Can you endure{H5375} the death{H4194} that I shall endure{H5375}, and the immersion{H2881} that I shall be immersed{H2881}?
And you shall be immersed{H2881}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew is extremely condensed — Greek has a fuller exchange: 'They said to him: We are able. And Yeshua said to them: You shall indeed drink of the cup... and be immersed.' The Hebrew preserves only Yeshua's concluding statement.

verses.translation: But to sit{H3427} at my right{H3225} and at my left{H8040} is not mine to give{H5414} to you, but to those for whom it is prepared{H3559}.
And when the ten{H6235} disciples heard{H8085} it, they were full{H4392} of wrath{H2534} against Ya'aqov{H3290} and Yochanan{H3110}.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses חימה (chemah — 'wrath/fury', H2534) where Greek has ἠγανάκτησαν ('were indignant'). Same pattern as v14 — the Hebrew emotion is divine fury, not mere annoyance.

verses.translation: And Yeshua called{H7121} them and said{H559} to them: You know{H3045} that the rulers{H8269} and the authorities{H7980} — the great ones{H1419} rule{H4910} over the small{H6996}, and their officers{H8269} have great{H1419} power{H3581} over the small{H6996}.
It shall not be so among you. The one who wishes{H7521} to be great{H1419} shall be your servant{H5650}.
And the one who seeks{H2664} to be first{H7223} shall be your minister{H8334}.
And the Son{H1121} of God{H430} comes to you for the sake of serving{H5647} and for the sake of giving{H5414} his soul{H5315} as a ransom{H6306} for many{H7227}.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses בן האלוה (ben ha-eloah — 'Son of God') where Greek has υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man').

Uses פדיון (pidyon — 'ransom/redemption', H6306). This is the specific Torah redemption price — the ransom for the firstborn (Num 3:46-49, 18:15-16), the ransom for a life (Ex 21:30). Greek has λύτρον ('ransom'). While equivalent, the Hebrew word carries the full firstborn-redemption theology of the Torah.
translation_notes: 'Ransom' for pidyon — the Torah's redemption price. Yeshua gives his soul as the pidyon — the firstborn-redemption price — for the many.
textual_notes: Numbers 18:15: 'Everything that opens the womb... you shall redeem (תפדה)... the redemption price (פדיון) you shall pay.' The Son of God pays the firstborn's redemption price.

verses.translation: And they came{H935} to Yericho{H3405}, and entered{H935} Yericho{H3405} with his disciples and a great{H7227} people{H5971}; and the son of Timai, Bar-Timai, who was withered{H3001}, sat{H3427} near{H7138} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יבש (yavesh — 'withered/dried up', H3001). Greek has τυφλός ('blind'). The Hebrew says the man was WITHERED, not BLIND. Different affliction entirely. The verb יבש describes a dried/withered condition — like the withered hand in Mark 3:1 or Ezekiel's dry bones (Ezek 37:2). A back-translator from 'blind' would use עור (iver — 'blind'), not יבש.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'withered' (יבש — dried up). Greek: 'blind' (τυφλός). Different disability.

verses.translation: And he began to cry out{H6817} and said{H559}: Son{H1121} of David{H1732}, have compassion{H2550} on me!
And Yeshua stood{H5975} and called{H7121} him; and they called{H7121} him and said{H559} to him: Behold{H2009}, Yeshua asks{H7592} for you.
And he cast away{H7993} his garments{H4403} and immediately came{H935} to him.
And Yeshua said{H559} to him: Go{H1980}, for your faith{H530} has saved{H3467} you. And immediately he saw{H7200} and followed{H4900} after him on the way{H1870}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הושיעך (hoshi'akha — 'has saved you', from ישע H3467 — 'to save'). This is the root of Yeshua's own name (ישוע). The wordplay: Yeshua (ישוע) says 'your faith has SAVED (הושיע) you' — the salvation is embedded in the Savior's name.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 10 in Hebrew contains several major one-way markers. (1) נפילים (Nephilim, v33) replaces Greek 'gentiles' — the Hebrew author views the Romans as the biblical Nephilim, the violent fallen giants of Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33. No back-translator would replace 'gentiles' with 'Nephilim.' (2) ספר כריתות ('letter of cutting-off/divorce', v4) preserves the Deuteronomic legal terminology with its covenant-cutting metaphor. (3) בן האלוה/האל ('Son of God') again replaces 'Son of Man' in vv33 and 45. (4) יצר ('formed', v6) uses the Genesis 2:7 potter-verb rather than generic 'made.' (5) נחלות ('estates/inheritances', vv22,29) frames the rich man's wealth as tribal land-inheritance rather than generic possessions. (6) שפל ותמים ('humble and blameless', v15) adds two OT-loaded qualities absent from Greek. (7) משפחה ממאנת carries forward the 'refusing family' pattern. (8) באורך ('in your light', v37) again replaces Greek 'in your glory.' (9) Bar-Timai is described as יבש ('withered') not 'blind' — a completely different affliction. The chapter also preserves the Garden of Eden / Gei-Hinnom eschatological geography from chapter 9 by implication, and the פדיון ('ransom/redemption', v45) invokes the Torah's firstborn-redemption price for Yeshua's self-offering.
